detail.longDescription: at the first international agribusiness conference in 1967: "Senator McGovern termed the War on Hunger “an enlightened society’s substitute for colonialism.”" 😬 He said, “Great powers in the past have extended their defense and economic perimeters by subduing and exploiting peoples, investing their own wealth chiefly in the military might necessary to conquer, police, and defend their empires. We have the opportunity to make investments in productive resources instead of force, to build ourselves allies instead of colonies, and to benefit through trade and the enhanced security within a free world society." 😬 "He continued, “A problem that American enterprise will face in foreign lands is an inevitable suspicion of neocolonialism. It is a suspicion that must be overcome with reasonable capital returns, a dedication to growth with and not at the expense of host countries. Our own government’s backing will be needed for your service through full guarantees against the unusual risk of expropriation and unstable governments, a reasonable sharing of other risks, and supplemental government-to-government programs. These would include food aid and educational programs which will help clear away the impediments to your success.”" from the June 5, 1967 issue of "foreign agriculture": https:// archive.org/details/sim_foreig n-agriculture_1967-06-05_5_23/page/8/mode/2up so according to this, government was very much in favor of clearing the way for american agribusiness to enter developing country markets, and they framed it as "the role of private enterprise in the global war on hunger." did they actually believe that? it's certainly possible. does that change how we should view the impact of what they did? i don't think so. why am i still curious whether they were "true believers"? i dunno...i guess it's interesting to me to see how deeply misguided true believers - who also considered themselves "liberal" and "enlightened" - can go so wrong... i guess that's high modernism for ya! (see: james c. scott's "seeing like a state") for earlier posts on the subject of the green revolution and american neo-colonialism, see: https:// tilde.zone/@mk30/1171367784638 35809 # agriculture # history # colonialism # USHistory # GreenRevolution # research
